prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, and the experimental discovery of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I keep the configuration I moved to in round 1: a single-part prize for B018 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. Having read the full exchange, my reasons are the ones I care about as a theorist. The core result is a simple, general mechanism: time-reversal symmetry plus spin-orbit coupling gives a Z2 invariant, and a nontrivial value forces a protected helical edge. It was stated cleanly, made a sharp, checkable prediction (edge conductance of about 2e^2/h in a short sample), and nature confirmed it in HgTe wells in 2007, followed by about two decades of independent transport, ARPES and STM work in several material families. It is understood as well as observed, which matters to me as much as that it works. The convergence of six members from different fields is informative, but I do not count it as merit; I count that no supporter has found a scientific flaw and that the credited trio is the same in every configuration. On the chair's question about wording, I propose a narrow citation: the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 insulators, with HgTe named. That is an honest claim the three names can carry, and the omissions are then stated limits of the citation, not hidden ones.
statement.case_against: The attribution gap is real and I do not think it can be argued away. The HgTe proposal of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang told the experimentalists where to look, Zhang died in 2018, and the 3D work (Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents, Hasan) is outside the three names. If the primary papers show that the experiment would not have been done without BHZ, then Molenkamp's share rests on an execution that followed another group's idea, and the citation must say 'observation' and not imply that he originated the proposal. Second, topological band theory descends from the Haldane model and the 2016 prize, so a committee could regard this as a refinement of recognised ideas; HgTe edge quantisation is also imperfect in long samples, and practical impact is still prospective. If the committee judges these points decisive, the better outcome is B041, which has a cleaner two-name credit, and not a broader topological prize that the three-person limit cannot support.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether the HgTe experiment honours Kane, Mele and Molenkamp or really the BHZ proposal that guided it, and says the committee should check the primary papers.
responses.response: I agree that this is the one factual question that could change the configuration, and I accept her point that I cannot call the omission only a fairness issue. My own reading is this: Kane and Mele supplied the general Z2 classification and the first quantum spin Hall prediction, while BHZ supplied the specific HgTe band-inversion platform that made a feasible experiment. Molenkamp's group had the HgTe growth and transport capability and tested a prediction that was, in outline, already general. So the experiment was necessary for the discovery, and the trio is defensible as the prediction of the effect plus its first observation, but I would not claim they exhaust the theory. I keep the three names and rely on the citation scope, and I would change my view only if the record shows the experiment was designed purely to test BHZ and not the Kane-Mele picture.

responses.point: The chair asks whether the 2016 prize (Thouless, Haldane, Kosterlitz) leaves room for a distinct time-reversal-invariant topological insulator prize, and asks condensed-matter members to answer.
responses.response: I am a statistical-physics theorist, not a band-theory specialist, so I answer as a user of these ideas. The 2016 prize rewarded topological invariants in the integer quantum Hall state, which needs a magnetic field or broken time reversal, and topological defects in two-dimensional phases. Z2 insulators are a different symmetry class in which protection comes from time-reversal symmetry alone and appears in ordinary non-magnetic materials, with no quantum Hall field. The Haldane model is the direct precursor of Kane-Mele, so I do not pretend the lineage is unrelated, but a symmetry-protected phase that is observed experimentally is a distinct, tested discovery and not a restatement. I also think the committee should say this in the citation by naming the quantum spin Hall effect, so that the prize cannot be read as a repeat of 2016.

responses.point: Eriksson supports the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp core as separable, and notes the topological case is incomplete on credit, while also asking about pairing B018 with the quantum anomalous Hall candidate B030.
responses.response: I agree that the core is separable, and that is why I resist broadening it. A topological prize wide enough to absorb the 3D insulators, the quantum anomalous Hall effect and the twisted-graphene correlated phases would be a prize for a field, with arbitrary cuts forced by the three-person limit. I would also not pair B018 with B030 now: the twisted-bilayer case is younger and its superconducting pairing mechanism is not settled, which is the concern Eriksson himself raised. A single, narrowly worded part is the more defensible choice. He also answered my B032 position fairly, and I accept his point that the exact fluctuation relations were largely confirmed in experiments rather than surprising us, so I do not push B032 further this round.

responses.point: Kroll prefers B041 for the clean Katori-Ye credit and the new measurement capability, but states the objection that it may be a second-generation improvement after the 2005 and 2012 prizes and that the priority among Katori, Ye and other groups is unverified.
responses.response: I take B041 seriously as the best alternative, and I agree the two-name credit is cleaner than for B018. My difficulty is the one Kroll raises himself. The decisive idea, the magic wavelength, is Katori's, and Ye's role is largely the performance frontier, so a two-name citation would either rest on a priority judgement that members admit they recall only from memory, or credit capability and not discovery. The physics payoff so far consists of constraints and null results. If he or Lindroth can formulate a citation that names the lattice concept as the discovery, I would want to see it. Until then I put it second, behind B018, where nature surprised us with a new class of insulator.

uncertainties: Whether the primary papers show that the HgTe experiment was designed specifically to test Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, which would weaken Molenkamp's independent credit.
Whether a citation limited to the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 insulators is accepted as a fair account without the 3D work of Fu, Moore, Balents and Hasan.
Whether the 2016 topological-phases prize is judged to leave room for this prize, which depends on a condensed-matter judgement I can only make as an interested theorist.
My recollection of priority dates is from memory and not checked against the primary literature.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Katori, Ye or Jarzynski, Evans and Seifert is apparent from my profile, and I know of no collaboration with any credited name. I share the Gothenburg physics environment (GU and Chalmers) with Johansson and Olsson, and Johansson has disclosed ties to the circuit-QED candidate B020, which is not in my configuration, so my disclosure is unchanged from round 1.
